subject: history_social
passage: Obsidian, a volcanic glass that can be chipped into sharp blades, was prized by ancient toolmakers, and each volcanic source has a chemical signature that lets archaeologists trace a tool back to its origin. Archaeologist Rosa Mendieta analyzed obsidian tools from a settlement in central Mexico across four periods of its occupation. She argued that the settlement's trade links reached farther over time, as tools made from distant sources made up a growing share of the total.

data.title: Origin of Obsidian Tools from a Settlement in Central Mexico, by Period

stem: Which choice most effectively uses data from the table to support Mendieta's argument?

choices.A: Obsidian from distant sources was of higher quality than obsidian from sources near the settlement.
choices.B: Tools from sources within 100 kilometers made up the majority of the tools analyzed in every period.
choices.C: The share of tools from sources within 100 kilometers rose steadily across the four periods.
choices.D: The share of tools from sources more than 300 kilometers away rose from 2 percent in the earliest period to 19 percent in the latest.

explanation.why: Mendieta's argument is that distant sources supplied a growing share of tools over time. The support must track a far-source share across the periods: the share from sources over 300 kilometers away rose from 2 to 6 to 12 to 19 percent (and the 100–300 kilometer share also grew).
explanation.A: Incorrect. The table shows where tools came from, not how good the obsidian was.
explanation.B: Incorrect. This is true, but it emphasizes how much local obsidian was used and says nothing about whether distant sources grew.
explanation.C: Incorrect. This reverses the data: the local share fell from 88 percent to 52 percent; it did not rise.
explanation.D: Correct. A share rising from 2 percent to 19 percent across the four periods shows distant sources becoming more important, as Mendieta argues.
